projects.name: Fires
projects.write_up: After The Eaton Fire:  Works created in response to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. The Eaton wildfire hit very close to home, as I've lived in and around this community for my entire life.  The experience of seeing our neighborhoods, mountains, and a lifetime of memories tied to a place, go up in flames overnight was one I will never forget.  Finding ways to work with this subject has been a challenge.  Some images and memories are too difficult to face. Yet, I keep returning to images and memories of people gathering and helping, showing kindness, solidarity, and overwhelming generosity.
projects.synopsis: Works created in response to the 2025 Eaton Wildfire

projects.name: Daciaramă-Panorama
projects.write_up:
This series of photographic artworks are created through a unique and complex process.  They originate with a digital i-phone panorama photograph, taken through the window of a moving car, with all of its visual glitches and distortions.  This image is printed out on paper, transferred by hand to a plastic adhesive transparency, and then chemically printed in the darkroom onto black-and-white photographic paper.  These works are part of a larger series of digital-to-analogue photographs.

The name Daciaramă plays with the words "Dacia" and "ramă." Dacia is both the ancient name for the geographic region of Romania, as well as a make of popular Romanian automobile; and ramă, means window frame in Romanian.  These photos were taken while driving throughout the roads and small towns in western Romania, a region where the traditional analogue world collides with, sometimes resists, and exists in spite of, the modern digital world.
projects.synopsis: A series of analogue photographs made through the window of a moving car, capturing the landscapes and small towns of western Romania as a shifting, dreamlike collision between the old and the new.

projects.name: The Storyteller
projects.write_up:
The Storyteller is a series of video slideshows constructed from photographs found in my grandparents’ collections, dating from the 1950s through the 1980s. The photographs at times recall memorable moments from family history, and at other times are blurry, accidental photographs that my grandparents kept nonetheless. Most of the images’ original circumstances, meanings, and stories are only partly known, becoming the starting points for stories about strange and sometimes improbable encounters with animals. 

In the space between image and text, fact and fiction, memory and invention, the photographs become something other than evidence: they become witnesses, clues, and openings through which another story can emerge, invoking a world in which humans are no longer the only storytellers.
projects.synopsis: A series of video slideshows made from found photographs. Images become clues for strange and sometimes improbable animal encounters, inhabiting the uncertain space between fact and fiction, memory and invention, and human and nonhuman ways of seeing.

projects.name: Saltanimals
projects.write_up: Saltanimals is a multi-paneled work featuring tiny animals are hand-painted in salt water on black paper. As the water dries, the unique crystalline structure of the Dead Sea water and the Great Salt Lake water becomes visible. The properties of these salt water sources have continued to change and respond to the work's environment over the years, at times, re-liquifying, changing color, and taking on a life of their own. Saltanimals has become the subject of a collaborative study by crystallographer Dr. Gili Cohen-Taguri and paper conservator Noa Cahaner-McManus, and is featured in a display at the NANO Fetter Museum of Nanoscience and Art.
projects.synopsis: Constellations of tiny animals hand-painted in crystallized salt water

projects.name: Geomagnetic Travellogue
projects.write_up:
This project follows the zero-degree line of the
earth's magnetic field from the year 1590.
It is a work in progress.

The year 1590 is significant, as it coincides with the
development of Galileo's first telescope, and with the
creation of the first compound microscope.

Therefore, my project explores incidences of macro-
and micro-scopic vision, magnetic attraction and
polarity, and the intersection of scientific, historical,
and artistic narratives.

On May 10, 2008 I made my first journey. I would attempt to go to Peru, Iceland, South Africa, and Australia.

I started my expedition in Los Angeles, and after carefully studying my maps, I plotted my destinations. I had 24 hours to make this trip.

*parallel worlds*\
*using the wrong map to get to the right places*\
*can I reach Peru through a looking glass?*
projects.synopsis: Tracing the zero-degree line of the earth's magnetic field from 1590 to the present, in five journeys.

children.name: Los Angeles
children.write_up:
I consider Los Angeles to be the starting and ending point for this journey. It is my birthplace, and I have lived here for most of my life. 

California is known for its earthquakes, and Los Angeles sits upon the San Andreas Fault. This important fault-line is where the Pacific tectonic plate slides past the North American tectonic plate. Half of Los Angeles is moving slowly towards Anchorage, Alaska. The other half is traveling south.

Los Angeles is home to Caltech, one of the foremost institutions in the study of seismic and geomagnetic activity, as well as astronomy and physics. Los Angeles is also home to the historical Mount Wilson Observatory, which is situated directly above my childhood home in Pasadena. The Mt. Wilson Observatory is where my grandfather accidentally met Edwin Hubble, and where Hubble made many of his notable observations with the now antiquated 100-inch Hooker Telescope.

children.write_up: An ancient lake bed is dotted with stones that mysteriously "move" leaving tracks in the earth. The Nazca earth drawings in Peru are similarly continuous pathways carved into the land. A large outcropping of rock sits at the north end of The Racetrack. Machupicchu was built across from a large rocky peack called Pachamama. Small scale models of this mountain can be found at Machupicchu. Perhaps the Incas understood the usefulness of the miniature and the mirror.

children.name: Cyprus
children.write_up:
The Mediterranean island of Cyprus has been inhabited since Neolithic times. The Greeks and the Turks have had conflict over the island for thousands of years. It is also the legendary birthplace of the Greek goddess of love, Aphrodite. The name "Cyprus" is probably a derivative of the Greek word for copper, which has been mined on the island since ancient times. This is probably the reason why Aphrodite/Venus is associated with the element copper.

It was not until November 1, 1974 (the exact day and year I was born) that a delicate peace agreement was reached for Cyprus. On this date, the U.N. drew a "green line" down the middle of the island, dividing it between the Greeks and the Turks.

children.title: Syrtos
children.write_up: The Syrtos is a dance with both Greek and Turkish origins. It features the unusual 7/4 rythym, and its steps create a spiraling movement. In nature, the spiral is a form that relieves and balances tension and opposition between two sides. The Syrtos can be danced in pairs or groups and is an expression of love and passion for life.

children.title: Double Cypriot
children.write_up: This painting, like Cyprus is divided in two. Yet, it attempts to bring two strong, beautiful, and ancient personalities into balance. The beehive that appears throughout my work is a reference to ancient mediterranean associations with bees and immortality. The Greeks believed that the immortal gods had honey flowing through their veins; they buried their dead in beehive-shaped tombs, and honey was recognized as a substance that had curative and preservative powers.

children.name: Back in the Studio
children.write_up:
Returning to the studio--

Reflections on travel, searching, and the illusiveness of a destination.

I began working with a square-ruled composition book. The idea of "the grid" as the surface and the history that I was treading on top of seemed a necessary starting point.

The page numbers, seemingly hand-stamped by some worker in the book factory interested me. The analogue "one number after another" sequence felt like a familiar companion through the long hours of travel. 

Once I unraveled the binding and separated the pages of the book, new relationships between the page numbers began to form. Page number one shared the same piece of paper as page number 152. The doldrums were found where page 126 leads to page 27.

This work is still in progress.

projects.name: The Intimacy of Physics
projects.write_up:
This series of work began with a handful of texts and images from the history of science: Galileo's experiments in physics, Captain James Cook's observations of the Transit of Venus, and various documents from the U.S. Geological Survey. I have layered these stories with my own, re-presenting and even re-enacting them in order to understand them on a more personal and direct level. This work could be seen as a desperate attempt to find hope, not in the rational certainty of science, but in its intuitive and transformative capacities.

I begin with a simple shift in the language of science, to reveal it for what it truly is: a poetry of intimacy, of falling bodies and celestial visions passing before the eyes of history.
projects.synopsis: Photographs, paintings, and objects that layer episodes from the history of science with personal narrative.

children.title: Transit of Venus
children.write_up: Between you and me something becomes visible; you are the backdrop that brings Venus into view. The "Transit of Venus" refers to the path that the planet Venus makes across the face of the Sun. When this event was observed by scientists in 1761, it became one of the earliest examples of international collaboration in the field of science. My photographs re-enact this astronomical phenomenon, but as an intimate gesture between two human beings.

children.title: Measuring the Distance at Which We Can No Longer Hear Each Other
children.write_up: When Tony and I collaborated on this art piece back in 2007, we thought we were measuring the acoustics of the desert. I asked him to hold one end of a piece of twine, and then walk into the landscape until we could no longer hear each other. Today I realize there are many distances at which people can no longer hear each other. There are voluntary distances, theoretical distances... the distances of ignorance and forgetfulness. There are geo-political distances that separate families and loved ones on each side of national boundaries; and for Tony and I, there remains the unfathomable distance of death, at which we will no longer be able to hear each other.

images.alt: Measuring the Distance at Which We Can No Longer Hear Each Other

projects.name: Blackboard
projects.write_up:
Blackboard presents a series of photos taken in an abandoned school building in Berkeley, California. In one of the classrooms, I discovered that the blackboard had a tiny crack down the middle of it. If you stood close enough, you could see a tiny line of light shining through from the other side.

If you put your eye right up to the crack, you could see right through the crack, all the way across the next room, to an open window with sun streaming through its white curtains.

My camera was set up on a tripod, right in front of this crack. With each photo, I adjust the focus slightly, which pushes the image from a crisp view of the flat blackboard, gradually passing through the crack, across the next room behind the board, and finally ending at the open window in the distance.
projects.synopsis: A still camera in an abandoned classroom: A cracked blackboard becomes a tiny aperture, a passage between spaces and scales.

projects.name: Department of Nocturnal Affairs (D.N.A.)
projects.write_up:
The D.N.A. is a creative project by artists Caroline Maxwell and Tal Yizrael. Envisioned as both a work of installation and performance art, the DNA functions as a speculative bureaucracy and a precarious archive. The DNA has opened field offices in various public spaces around Los Angeles and the world to collect reports of nocturnal wildlife encounters.

Caroline Maxwell has created multiple artworks in conjunction with D.N.A. projects over the years.
projects.synopsis: A collaborative installation and performance project, collecting reports of nocturnal wildlife encounters, and investigating darkness as a fertile ground for knowledge and memory.

children.name: Sholem Asch House Museum: Nocturnal Residency
children.write_up:
The D.N.A. were artists in residence at the Sholem Asch House Museum in 2020. As resident artists, the D.N.A. transformed the home of Yiddish essayist and playwright Sholem Asch through various installations that explore darkness as a theme. 

Because of the covid pandemic, the residency had to be attended remotely. Photographs of the space, and surveillance camera images produced nocturnal views of the house that became source material for many artworks.
children.synopsis: Artworks created for a residency at the Sholem Asch House Museum, 2020.

children.title: Portrait Companions: Badger With Eyes Closed by Caroline Maxwell (2020); Woman With Eyes Closed by Maurycy Gottlieb (late 1800s).
children.write_up: A particular portrait that hangs on the wall of Asch's house, a portrait of a woman with her eyes closed, has become a centerpiece for the D.N.A. residency. Why is this woman closing her eyes? Where has she gone in this darkened moment? She understands the uses of darkness, of closing one thing to open another. Part of a set of companion portraits, depicting nocturnal animals with closed eyes to join this woman on her journey.

projects.name: San Andreas Project
projects.write_up:
An installation at Claremont Graduate University, Oct. 30 - Nov. 5, 2006.

The San Andreas Fault is California's major earthquake fault. It is where the Pacific Tectonic Plate slides past the North American Plate. This installation interprets and misinterprets the significance of geo-tectonic activity.
projects.synopsis: An installation at Claremont Graduate University interpreting and misinterpreting the significance of geo-tectonic activity.

children.write_up: Photo by G.K. Gilbert, U.S. Geological Survey.

children.title: Fort Tejon Corral
children.write_up: In 1857, the Fort Tejon Earthquake on the San Andreas Fault resulted in a 30-foot displacement along the fault zone. A corral built directly on the fault line was changed from a circular shape to an s-shape — broken open.

children.title: Shovello
children.write_up: A shovel, like the one used in the accompanying video, is outfitted with cello strings. The strings measure 36.9 cm., which is the average distance the San Andreas Fault has moved since the day I was born. This personal measurement now creates a specific and personal tonal range for this instrument. The San Andreas fault is a lateral strike-slip fault. The correct way to play this instrument is with lateral strike-slip movements.

children.title: Powerlines
children.write_up: Copper wires transmit power and communication over great distances in an instant. Hair grows imperceptibly slowly. An earthquake fault moves imperceptibly slowly, and on occasion, extremely powerfully. These powerlines represent both of these energies together.

children.title: Dig
children.write_up: Two video images, Mojave Desert. I continuously dig a hole, and carry the dirt offscreen towards the corner of the room. Within a smaller video image, a mountain begins to grow as I move the dirt from the hole on the right, and pile it up in the image on the left.

items.name: Flames, After Botticelli
items.synopsis: Originally appeared in the 2026 anthology Burned: Stories about Fire, Real and Imagined. This essay follows an arc of fire through time, layering Dante, Botticelli, astrophysics, pandemic isolation, and the landscape of Altadena, connecting historical imagery and literature with personal experience of the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. Like much of my visual work, it is an attempt to follow a series of seemingly disparate clues to discover what they reveal when brought into relation with one another.
items.write_up:
Published in the Anthology "Burned:Stories About Fire" (2025) Edited by Nicholas Davidge and Alana White

[Leader.jpg]

Where do stories begin, and where do they end?  Fresh chapters and revelations always arrive by their own timetables.  Some stories return again and again to our world, and sometimes, we only have to look for the clues, and listen to recognize their voices. This story begins with an ending. It’s a travelog of sorts, that traverses a personal and temporal landscape, tracing an arc of fire through time, with Dante as a guide. 

We begin in July of 2020, during the worldwide Covid Pandemic. We were all living a bizarre bubble-life of a quarantine lockdown, and one of the places I would often escape to was the Hahahmonga Watershed Park, at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains, in Altadena, California.  An odd place, not quite park, not quite wilderness, it’s a space where the natural world and human-made infrastructure coexist in peculiar proximity. The area consists of roads and trails circling a large dam and seasonal wetlands. A river flows right down the middle from the mountains above.  These waters split off, and are partially diverted through a series of channels, locks, and ponds. All of these waters culminate at a massive concrete reservoir, known by the local name, “Devil’s Gate Dam.”  The park is traversed by local hikers, horseback riders, birdwatchers, and mountain bikers, along with municipal water district employees that maintain this series of channels and ponds.  The entire park sits alongside the massive campus of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, its own mountain of buildings rising up against the chaparral slopes of the Angeles National Forest.

[DevilsGate.jpg]

During the pandemic, many of us found ourselves in a strange space of isolation, needing to reach for, and re-forge our connection with others in new ways.  The acute awareness of our short history as humans on this planet, the plagues and pandemics that have inevitably shaped our lives and losses, strengthened a fresh kinship for me personally, with those artists, astronomers, and writers of the past, who strove to form a better world out of the ashes, the plagues, and upheavals of their times.

I remembered the drawings by Sandro Botticelli I had seen years earlier, of Dante and Beatrice rising up through the stars, traversing the spheres of heaven. Narrated by the lines of Dante’s Divine Comedy,  Botticelli’s stars appeared like immaculately patterned and animated fires, forming and reforming at each successive level of Paradise.  To Dante, as well as Botticelli, these blazing stars were each a representation of the divine, and are simultaneously, “the living power within our own hearts… what holds the earth together.” (Canto 1 - Paradiso)  These words struck a deep chord for Dante and his readers. Dante drew from the suffering and agony of his own personal life, living years in exile from his home, while witnessing the horrors of wars and plagues.  From the tormenting flames of the Inferno, to the emotional suffering and regret of Purgatorio; at the end of his poetic journey, it was the distillation of all this loss and pain in his heart, that reveals the love that still remains and lights the way to Paradise.  

[birds.jpg]

As I spent my days of quarantine walking through this park alone, I wondered how odd it was, that right in front of me, astrophysicists were reaching for and receiving signals from distant stars.  I wondered, to what end will all of this signaling lead? And how are we, standing here today, a bridge between the past and the future humans who have always, and will always, be signaling stars?

While tormenting fires existed in Dante’s Inferno, they were small and individual, and Hell was a cold, hard place.  In Purgatorio, we are confronted with fire again; it is horrifying and all-consuming, yet it offers purification and redemption on a deeper level.  When Dante reaches this wall of fire upon his final ascent through Purgatory, he feels a greater terror than ever before, knowing that he has to pass through this intense flame, becoming all but ash, in order to be renewed.  When he emerges on the other side, he has left his fears behind. 

 In Paradiso he is greeted again by flames, but now they are pure light, living spirits, dancing, animated by love itself.  Looking back, all earthly existence seems as “strange as a flame that never moves.”  (Canto 1 - Paradiso)

The year before the Covid pandemic, I had painted a page of these heavenly fires, after Botticelli. I was staying in a small town in Italy, not far from where Dante and Botticelli had envisioned their own flaming stars.  As I walked down the local streets, past the cafes and bars with their ads for ice creams and mobile phones, I imagined my page of Botticelli’s fires printed onto large sheets of wallpaper, covering the walls and billboard signs that filled the countryside with their commercial signals.  One day, I printed twenty-five sheets of my flame drawings and pasted them onto a small, vacant billboard that stood along a narrow road by an olive grove.  It felt like a message, a signal fire sent out into the world.

[Botticelli.jpg]

On my walks through Hahahmonga park in the summer of 2020, I began to notice a number of old trail signs and markers, many of which were empty or so weathered that their markings had disappeared under the sun of passing years.  I gathered my pages of Botticelli’s flames, and posted them onto these guideposts around the park.  There, in the shadow of NASA, stood these guideposts to the stars, like small beacons against the darkness, hope in a pandemic.

My connection with Botticelli’s fires didn’t begin with my stay in Italy. It was actually a few years earlier, when a friend had traveled to London, and visited the Courtauld Gallery to see Botticelli’s illustrations for the Divine Comedy.  Upon return, she had given me a gift, a small print of Dante and Beatrice rising through the Second Planetary Sphere of Paradise.  Here, the two beloved reach towards each other, encircled by concentric rings of flaming stars.  This print has hung on my wall since 2016, always quietly in the background of life. 

Just a few months ago, this same friend rushed back to Los Angeles on a flight from Miami.  Her family’s home in Altadena was in the path of the Eaton Wildfire.  Countless homes and businesses in the community had already been lost.  On January 8, I walked over to my friend’s house to check on her parents, who had remained home throughout the wildfires.  Fortunately, their home was spared much damage, but their yard was littered with ash and debris that was still blowing in with the high winds and surrounding fires.  As I was leaving, a burned page from a book drifted down from the wind above me, and landed at my feet in the driveway.  A small illustration graced this page from a fairy tale, showing a young woman– who looked strikingly like my friend, or was it Beatrice?  The edges of the page were neatly burned, almost too perfectly, by this monstrosity of a fire that delivered so many endings in such a short amount of time. This strange arrival seemed to remark that the mythic is always close at hand in times of crisis. 

[BurnPage.jpg]

After these devastating wildfires, many of us have found ourselves in darkness, like Dante, exiled from our homes.  We can return, but never in the same way.  How can one be haunted by fire? These are not the cold ghosts that shimmer in the darkness– here we are haunted by raging, incendiary specters, burning with the heat of exploding stars. This story begins with an ending, when seemingly all has been lost.  Or perhaps, caught between beginnings and endings, learning that the only path ahead is through fire and grief.  As I write this on Good Friday, I’m aware that this is also the day that Dante’s story begins. And so we shall begin, in the darkness, at the doorway to the Inferno, Devil’s Gate Dam.

[GatewayTrees.jpg]
